analysis.one_liner: Spends on removing lead pipes and taps from homes, paid for by ending carried-interest and estate-tax breaks.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in July 2026 with one cosponsor and sent to three House committees; no committee or floor vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill authorizes $9.5 billion a year for ten years in grants to states and cities to find and remove lead-based pipes, taps, and fixtures from homes, with priority for low-income housing [S2]. It requires lead-pipe inspections and cleanup in federally assisted housing, adds disclosure rules for anyone selling or renting a home, and sets training and certification standards for abatement contractors [S2]. To pay for it, the bill ends the carried-interest tax break for investment fund managers, taxes partnership interests given in exchange for services as ordinary pay, and returns the estate and gift tax exemption to its pre-2018 level [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: Children under 6 and their families, especially in low-income and federally assisted housing, get lead hazards found and removed; homebuyers and renters get mandatory disclosure of known lead-pipe hazards; communities get federal grants plus a 10 percent local match to do the work.

how_it_helps.text: The bill authorizes $9.5 billion each fiscal year from 2026 through 2035 for HUD grants to evaluate and reduce lead-based pipe hazards in housing, with a 10 percent local match required and priority given to projects protecting young children [S2].

It requires periodic risk assessments and abatement in federally assisted housing, with initial assessments covering at least half of the units within five years, and lets Section 8 rents be adjusted to cover abatement costs [S2].

It requires sellers and landlords to disclose known lead-pipe hazards before a sale or lease is binding, gives buyers a 10-day window to test, and imposes civil penalties and triple damages on violators [S2].

It directs federal money toward the removal of lead pipes and taps, which are a recognized cause of childhood lead poisoning, a condition that causes permanent neurological damage, learning disabilities, and lower IQ in young children [S2].

The bill pays for the program by repealing preferential tax treatment for carried interest — the fund-manager share of investment gains taxed at capital-gains rates — treating it as ordinary income instead, which raises revenue from a small group of high earners [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Fund managers and investment partnerships, who lose the carried-interest break and would owe ordinary income tax rates on their share of investment gains; large estates, which face the pre-2018 lower tax exemption; and landlords and sellers, who face disclosure, inspection, and abatement costs.

drawbacks.text: The bill spends roughly $95 billion over ten years, and Section 302 authorizes unspecified additional sums for EPA lead work; it is paid for by new taxes that its critics would call a tax increase on investment management and wealthy estates [S2].

Mandatory disclosure of lead-pipe hazards and required abatement during federally funded renovations could add costs to home sales and renovations, which sellers, landlords, and the real estate industry would likely pass on to buyers and renters [S2].

Requiring all abatement work to be done by certified contractors raises the cost of lead cleanup, and the return of the pre-2018 estate tax exemption would apply to estates that include family businesses and farms [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit — removing lead from drinking-water plumbing in homes where young children live — addresses a well-documented cause of irreversible harm to children, and the bill names its own revenue sources rather than adding to the deficit. The costs are real but narrower: higher taxes on fund managers and large estates, and compliance costs in housing transactions. The main design weakness is not the trade-off but the politics: a bill pairing a large spending program with repeal of two tax breaks prized by high earners has no visible path in the current House.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees the day it was introduced, and no committee has taken up the bill since.

narrative.text: Representative Shontel Brown introduced the bill on July 22, 2026, joined by Representative Rashida Tlaib, the bill's sole cosponsor [S1] [S3].
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce, Financial Services, and Ways and Means Committees; the action history shows no further steps — no hearing, markup, or vote — since that day [S4].

The revenue provisions sit in the Ways and Means Committee's jurisdiction, and the bill's lead-grant program sits in Energy and Commerce and Financial Services, so no single committee has yet taken responsibility for moving it [S1] [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has yet gained or lost, because the bill has not moved; if it dies in committee, the beneficiaries are the fund managers and large estates whose tax breaks the bill would have repealed, and landlords and sellers who would have faced disclosure and abatement mandates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; tax breaks stand

for.name: Shontel M. Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the GET THE LEAD OUT Act on July 22, 2026, pairing a $9.5 billion-per-year lead-pipe abatement program with repeal of the carried-interest and estate-tax breaks [S1] [S4].

for.name: Rashida Tlaib
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction [S2] [S3].

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the lone cosponsor are Democrats, and the record shows no Republican support or any vote on the bill, so no partisan split has been measured.

industries.industry: Private equity and hedge fund managers
industries.note: The bill treats carried interest and partnership interests given for services as ordinary income, ending a tax preference that lets fund managers pay capital-gains rates on compensation for their work. Its repeal is the bill's main pay-for, so the industry's tax benefit is directly what funds the public program [S2].

Federal grants and mandatory abatement in federally assisted housing create paid work for certified lead-removal contractors, and the bill funds state training and certification programs to build that workforce [S2].

Sellers and landlords must disclose known lead-pipe hazards, and abatement is required during federally funded renovation, adding compliance costs; but grant-funded abatement and Section 8 rent adjustments can cover the cost of the work in assisted housing [S2].

Returning the estate and gift tax basic exclusion to its pre-2018 level exposes more of the largest estates to tax; the benefit of the current higher exemption flows to a small group of very wealthy families [S2].

analysis.trajectory: A large spending bill whose revenue provisions raise taxes on investment managers and large estates, introduced late in the session by two Democrats with no other cosponsors and split across three committees, very rarely reaches the floor. Unless the committees schedule action in the remaining months of this Congress, the bill will expire in January 2027 without a vote.
